# 言语·沟通·表达 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 12 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景：**左栏**读短文（目标词加粗），**右栏**常驻该篇生词释义，可先猜后对照。



### When the Room Decides to Speak

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The committee had gathered to debate a **compendium** of new communication guidelines. The chair called for a vote — the **aye**s won, narrowly beating the **nay**s — so someone **jot**ted the result on a whiteboard before the **nag**ging minority could reopen the argument. One dissenter muttered "**nah**," crossed her arms, and stared at the ceiling. A colleague leaned over: "The **gist** is simple — we need clearer language. **Viz**, no more **cant**, no more **guff**." She gave a reluctant **beck** of the head, conceding the point.

Across the hall, the communications team was rehearsing a product launch. The draft script was full of **hype** — breathless adjectives, every sentence a **rave** — so the editor began to **carp**, circling the worst lines in red. "This reads like a **brag**," she said. "Cut the **slur** against the rival brand. Don't **mock** the competition. Just **laud** what we actually built." The copywriter, who had been half-listening while scrolling through a **meme** feed, finally looked up. A junior writer dropped a quiet **hint** that the whole opening was recycled **adage**s dressed up as insight — true enough that no one laughed.

Later, over coffee, the mood loosened into ordinary **chat**. Someone spun a long **yarn** about a conference call that devolved into a **rant** when the presenter's audio began to **hiss** mid-sentence and the **honk** of street traffic swallowed his punchline. He had switched to **Urdu** out of frustration — a language none of the other callers shared — before finally hanging up. The story got funnier with each retelling. A linguist at the table noted that "**Urdu**" contains a rich tradition of courtly rhetoric, then pivoted to explaining how a **conj** — a **noun** of logical relation — could single-handedly change the meaning of an entire clause. She picked up her phone to **dial** a colleague who would appreciate the point. Nobody minded the tangent. That's how good conversation works: one word pulls the next, and meaning arrives before anyone planned it.
:::

### The Morning Scoop

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Before the editorial meeting, Dana sat down with her **diary** to **draft** a quick **recap** of the week's stories. The big **scoop** — a whistleblower account she'd been nursing for days — was finally ready to go to **print**. She had planned to write a measured **op-ed**, but her editor wanted a front-page splash instead. A **rumor** was already circulating online, and if they waited, a rival outlet would **blurt** it out first.

She read her notes aloud, and the **irony** wasn't lost on her: a story about silence, told in the loudest possible voice. She used a **caret** to mark a missing clause, swapped a **comma** for a dash, and paused to **parse** every sentence with the same care a linguist brings to an unfamiliar **lingo**. One paragraph felt too self-congratulatory — she had wanted to **extol** the whistleblower's courage without sounding like a **bravo**-hungry cheerleader. She cut the lines where she'd tried to **exalt** her own reporting and tightened the **quote** she'd pulled from the source.

Down the hall, the night editor was already **growl**ing at the layout team; someone had let a **smear** of ink ruin the proof. A junior reporter began to **bleat** about deadlines. The **noise** of the newsroom — keyboards, arguments, a **siren** somewhere outside — pressed in from all sides. Dana's colleague Marcus, who covered South Asia and often slipped into **Hindi** when excited, let out a low **grunt** of approval when he saw her lede. "**Howdy**," he said, which was his ironic all-purpose greeting regardless of the hour. "**Hoots**," she shot back — her own borrowed interjection for *I couldn't care less about the hour either.*

She **liken**ed the final edit to tuning an instrument: you **ditto** nothing, carry nothing forward unchanged. Every **query** gets answered, every rumor verified, every **smear** either proved or cut. A good story, she believed, could **edify** a reader the way a good teacher does — not by shouting, but by showing. She filed the piece at 4 a.m., silenced her phone, and let the presses do the rest.
:::

### The Art of Getting Through to Someone

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
In the greenroom before a live panel, Mara and her co-host exchanged **banter** that kept the nerves at bay — teasing each other about last week's **typos** in the show notes, laughing at every **cackle** that slipped out when a joke landed wrong. She'd once written a **spoof** of the network's style guide, and the crew still quoted it. Such was the **byword** of their partnership: if you can't laugh at the craft, you've already lost the audience.

The moment the red light blinked on, the tone shifted. Mara would **assert** her thesis with quiet conviction, never resorting to the **clamor** of talking heads who mistake volume for authority. When her guest **alluded** to a controversial study, she did not let the **cliche** "the research is clear" slide past unchallenged; she chose to **debunk** the misreading point by point, drawing on a broad **corpus** of peer-reviewed work to support her case. Her producer could **vouch** for every citation — they had spent a morning combing sources together. "I can **attest** to every figure we use," Mara would **utter** before each taping, a small ritual that kept both of them honest.

Midway through the episode, a viewer question arrived via live chat, riddled with what looked like a **cipher** no one had asked to decode. The guest leaned forward to **beckon** the camera closer, as though proximity might clarify meaning. He began to **babble** — not from nerves but from genuine excitement — layering clause upon clause before Mara gently raised a hand. She needed him to **affirm** the single core point before the audience lost the thread. He **assented** without bruising, and the two **concurred** on a formulation that was honest and plain. To **assure** listeners that no nuance had been lost, Mara **alluded** briefly to the fuller argument and promised a link in the show notes — a quiet **tacit** agreement between host and guest that the detail mattered even if air-time did not allow it.

After the taping, the sound editor flagged a segment where a troll in the live chat had sent a **spoof** account comment — little more than a malicious **tilde** decorating a fake handle — attempting to **accost** the guest with a distorted quote. The editor had already blocked the account. A researcher drafted a short thread to **deride** the misquote publicly, but the guest shook his head: better to **confer** with the legal team before publishing anything, and better still to let the **beacon** of an accurate transcript speak for itself rather than **bicker** with bad-faith actors. He had been **berated** once, years ago, by an editor who said arguing with trolls was the fastest way to make a **cliche** of yourself. He'd never forgotten it. The show would **troll** no one back; it would simply keep doing the work.
:::

### When Words Refuse to Stay Still

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
A retired diplomat once sat down to **peruse** the **scroll** of handwritten dispatches she had kept since her first posting abroad. Fifty years of foreign service, and yet the act of reading her own sentences still felt like meeting a stranger. She had spent decades trying to **impart** something true across every border — not merely facts, but feeling. In her early years she had relied on a **primer** of polite formulas, the kind every junior attaché was handed, full of **jargon** that was meant to smooth negotiations but mostly produced a kind of **pidgin** diplomacy: fluent on the surface, hollow underneath.

She remembered the interpreter who could **elicit** a confession from a stone — a quiet man whose every **remark** seemed to **evince** both patience and precision. He never needed to **holler** or **shriek** to be heard. He never let **rumors** rattle his composure, even when the room filled with the **hoopla** of competing delegations. When a junior colleague tried to **palter** over the wording of a joint statement, the interpreter simply waited, then offered one clean sentence that made all the **ironic** hedging unnecessary. Colleagues who tried to **retort** or **refute** his readings usually found themselves outflanked by their own words.

The ambassador herself had been less measured. She recalled **exhort**ing a young **scribe** not to **rattle** off minutes without listening first. She had once **recite**d a draft treaty clause aloud in the council chamber, only to hear a deputy **jangle** his pen against the table and mutter that the phrasing was a **herald** of trouble. He was right. The **outcry** from the opposition press was swift, and even the sympathetic coverage carried an edge of **gossip** that no official statement could fully **rebuff**. She had learned, slowly, that **praise** was a currency easier spent than earned, and that a single badly **indent**ed paragraph — a clause buried where no one would look — could unravel months of goodwill.

Now she was writing her **memoir**. She did not want it to **squeak** through history as a footnote. She wrote without the **scroll** of social media prompting her, without an audience ready to **rebuff** or applaud. The first sentence had taken her three weeks. She crossed out every word that felt borrowed, every phrase that seemed lifted from the official **jargon** she had spent a career navigating. What remained, she hoped, was something a reader could hold: honest, a little **ironic**, and entirely her own.
:::

### The Story That Leaks Out

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The debrief was supposed to be **concise**. Colonel Marsh had **briefed** his team in plain terms: say nothing beyond the mission summary, add the usual **caveats** about sources, and do not **digress** into personal opinion. Yet the moment the junior analyst opened her mouth, everyone sensed she was about to **unveil** something the room had not expected.

She did not **conceal** the numbers. She did not **distort** the timeline. She simply read aloud, in the flat cadence of someone who had rehearsed honesty, how the **courier** had failed to arrive, how the signal **beacons** had gone dark before dawn, and how a single mistranslated **acronym** had cascaded into the wrong order being issued. The colonel tried to **dismiss** the finding; she met his look and refused to let him. He was forced to **concede**.

Outside the briefing room, the story began its second life. One aide, known for **tattle** more than discretion, had already begun to **divulge** fragments to a journalist. Another would eventually **squeal** to an oversight committee. By evening, a blogger had clipped the video and added a sarcastic **caption**: "Watch an empire **dictate** its own collapse." A retired general delivered a **tirade** on cable news, insisting the entire account was fabricated to **conceal** institutional failure. The network ran the segment without a corrections **caption**, which only deepened the **dissent** online.

Meanwhile, the analyst tried to **clarify** her findings on the record. She had been trained in careful language — to **confide** only what evidence supported, never to **belabor** a point beyond what the audience needed. She knew the difference between a **dialect** of bureaucratic hedging and actual transparency. Her written statement cited an **Aramaic** inscription that had inspired the mission's code name, a detail she included to show how far back the **dispute** over the region went. Critics called the reference a distraction — a way to **disavow** present responsibility by burying it in ancient history.

She had consulted a linguist, used sources rendered in **Braille** format for an accessibility review, and still watched the **tirade**s mount. In the end she understood: language is a tool for precision, but **tattle** turns it into a weapon, and no matter how carefully you **consult** your own conscience, someone will always find a way to **distort** what you said into what you never meant.
:::

::::

### The Art of Making Oneself Understood

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Not everything is **effable** — yet the best communicators spend their lives hunting for words that come close. At the journalism **seminar** last spring, a veteran editor from **Reuters** opened with a provocation: in the age of the **tabloid** and viral **tidbits**, are we losing our ability to say what we actually mean? He had scribbled a single **jotting** on his notepad the night before: *precision matters*. He went on to **expound** on how **lexical** choices shape public perception, how a single word in a **leaflet** or a broadcast script can shift the entire **purport** of a message. The crowd, a mix of young **orators** and seasoned reporters, leaned in.

He didn't **espouse** any single style. Instead he drew on the full **lexicon** of rhetorical tradition — from the **literal** and plain to the ironic and **implied**. He used hand gestures, almost **emblems** in themselves, to show how much meaning travels outside words. At one point he **narrate**d a story about a colleague who was **scolded** by a senior producer for relying too heavily on **sarcasm** in a live segment — the audience had **hear of** the clip only through secondhand accounts and misread the tone entirely. "Sarcasm," he warned, "is the riskiest register." Someone in the back **mumbled** agreement; another **stammer**ed out a counterpoint before finding her footing.

The **preface** to his closing remarks addressed the darker side of public language. Editors must guard against **slander** and the slow rot of **traduce**-ment that bad-faith commentary can **instill** in audiences over time. The **rubrics** we use to evaluate good reporting — accuracy, fairness, clarity — exist precisely to block that drift. A journalist who **solicit**s quotes without context, or who lets **grumble**s about rivals color coverage, has already broken the contract with the reader. He ended with a quiet image: a correspondent standing in the rain, **hailing** a source who almost didn't show up, holding nothing but a notebook — and the belief that some things, however hard, remain **effable** enough to be worth saying.
:::

::::

### When Words Fill the Room

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The seminar had barely started when Professor Lin received a **wigging** from the department head for distributing an **abridged** edition of the course **analects** — an **anecdote** about administrative friction that quickly became legend among students. Her handout had paired **antonyms** in opposing columns, each row topped with an **aphorism** drawn from classical rhetoric. A small **asterisk** beside the title quietly pointed to a footnote: *adapted for classroom use*.

The graduate students, still **babbling** among themselves, settled when she began. One invited speaker that afternoon liked to **bloviate**, filling thirty minutes with what others said in five — pure **bollocks**, whispered the student in the back row. But the **bulletin** posted outside the room had promised a session on persuasion, and most had come in good faith. Lin spoke **candidly**, listing **cautions** against language that flatters rather than illuminates, against the **claptrap** politicians deploy when they want applause without commitment. "The way you **construe** a sentence," she said, "is the way you **convince** an audience — or lose them."

She reminded them never to **downplay** ambiguity with a careless **ellipsis**; an **eloquent** pause is not the same as evasion. An **enquirer** deserves a direct reply, not an **envelope** of vague qualifications. Be **explicit**, she urged — especially in **farewell** remarks, where every word lands heavier than expected. If danger looms, **forewarn**; do not wait until you are forced into a **harangue**. She paused, gave a dry **harrumph**, and added that every speaker carries an **idiolect** — a private fingerprint of syntax and rhythm — and that **innuendo** is merely the shadow cast when that fingerprint tries to hide something. "My job," she concluded, "is to **instruct** you not just in grammar, but in honesty."
:::

::::

### The Conference That Wouldn't End

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The **intercom** crackled to life at 7 a.m., jolting everyone in the press room awake. Dr. Reyes, a seasoned **linguist** and self-described **polyglot** fluent in six languages including **Sanskrit**, was already at the whiteboard. She had spent the night drafting a **synopsis** of the keynote and was quick to **jot down** last-minute notes in the margins, her handwriting teetering between neat cursive and outright **scribble**. The morning's theme was **literacy** — not merely the ability to read, but the deeper **semantic** command of language that separates a capable writer from a truly eloquent one.

When the first speaker took the stage, his **rhetoric** was polished but hollow, every second sentence edging into the **sermonic**. An audience member near the back groaned and muttered something — someone sitting beside her **overheard** it as *"pure **nonsense**."* The **narrator** of the opening film had used the word "groundbreaking" seventeen times, a **misnomer** if there ever was one for a panel rehashing ideas from a decade-old **treatise**. Still, the organizers had printed a slick **pamphlet** and a two-page **preamble** that tried, with mixed success, to **manifest** the conference's ambitions in concrete terms. A **metaphor** about rivers and language appeared in no fewer than three slides.

The real action was in the hallway. Over coffee, delegates began to **schmooze** — the polished kind, where every exchange is a rehearsed pitch. One junior researcher tried to **persuade** a journal editor to fast-track her **revision** of a disputed paper. The editor offered a quiet **rebuttal**, and when the researcher responded with thinly veiled **reproach**, a small crowd formed. Someone had even printed a rival **pamphlet** — a stapled, black-and-white affair — listing **synonyms** for "innovative" to mock the day's jargon. On the **landline** in the lobby, a harried publicist read from the official **synopsis** word for word, her tone flat. Outside, a dedicated **squealer** of a radiator pipe punctuated every pause. By afternoon the online chat had devolved into **trolling**, and the session chair, exhausted, called for **succinct** closing remarks — two minutes each, no extensions.
:::

### The Making of a Message

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
A young **columnist** sat at her desk, staring at a **facsimile** of an ancient **cuneiform** tablet her professor had once sent her — a reminder that humanity's impulse to communicate stretches back to the first scratched symbols. She was drafting a long **discourse** on how language shapes thought, and she wanted to open with something vivid rather than **anecdotal** evidence alone. Her argument's **predicate** was simple: every act of speech is also an act of power.

She had interviewed a veteran **publicist** that morning, a man famous for his skill at generating **publicity** for clients teetering on the edge of scandal. He answered her questions **brusquely**, barely pausing between **assertion** and counter-claim. At one point he lapsed into an extended **monologue** about reputation management — **or rather**, a polished performance of it — deploying **hyperbole** so fluently she had to **italicize** several of his quotes just to signal the rhetorical temperature to readers. When she asked whether he thought of himself as a mere **apologist** for bad behaviour, he cut her off: he was a **proponent** of narrative, he said, not a spin doctor. His publicist's instinct was to **propagate** a preferred story before a rival version could take root, to **inculcate** that story in every outlet willing to run it, and to **importune** every editor who hesitated.

Back at her desk she reached for a grammar handbook and looked up how an **adjective** could quietly tilt a sentence — the way a single modifier could carry more freight than a paragraph of plain statement. She noticed how she herself had started to **enunciate** her own views more carefully lately, aware that words, once on record, get **hand down** to audiences she would never meet. The piece would carry her **eponymous** byline, though she had once written under a **pseudonym** to protect a source. She used an **ampersand** to join two clauses in the headline — a small typographic choice — and watched the character count tick up. Outside, a pack of **Paparazzi** clustered below a hotel entrance, cameras ready; their subjects existed, **literally**, only as long as the lens agreed to find them. The **purported** star never emerged, but the photographers stayed, because the possibility of a picture is itself a kind of **adulation**, a silent insistence that someone is worth watching. She typed the final sentence, **designate**d the file for her editor, and closed the laptop.
:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::

### The Language of a Long Day

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
At the editorial board's year-end **symposium**, a junior editor rose to **reiterate** the team's standing rule: every **manuscript** submitted must include proper **annotation** and any supporting **appendices** before it enters review. She spoke **explicitly**, determined not to let ambiguity breed another round of corrections.

**By the way**, she added, the style guide had been updated — writers should no longer rely on **colloquial** phrasing when precision mattered, nor should they **exaggerate** a finding simply to **accentuate** its impact. Her tone was firm but never **accusatory**; she had no wish to seem **derogatory** toward the freelancers who had missed the mark. Still, she did not **repudiate** the criticism either. She read aloud a **memorandum** a senior editor had drafted — a **cautionary** note about a recent piece whose **discursive** structure had buried its argument under **ironically** verbose paragraphs.

A **dissenting** voice came from the back: a veteran writer who served as the magazine's unofficial **mouthpiece** for contributors. He argued, without trying to **contradict** the rule itself, that the new guidelines punished voice. One editor issued what amounted to a quiet **reprimand**, noting that a **compliment** for strong prose did not excuse weak sourcing. Someone consulting a **thesaurus** for every **vocabular** choice, another quipped, was not the same as thinking clearly. The **persuasion** that finally settled the room came from the editor-in-chief, who held up a draft page where a single **participle** had been misused across four **inscribing** passes without anyone catching it. The **revelator** of that small failure, she said, was not any one writer — it was the process. She handed out a revised one-pager, an **abridgment** of the full style manual, and suggested that **imputation** of blame helped no one. What mattered was that from this meeting forward, every editorial decision be made — and recorded — without **accusatory** hedging, without vague **imputation**, and without the kind of language that a reader could only parse as a coded **reprimand** buried in **compliment**.
:::

### When Words Fail — and When They Don't

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
A doctoral candidate sat in the archive, rifling through footnotes for her **dissertation**. She had spent months building her **bibliography**, cross-checking every source against the **encyclopedia** of linguistics her advisor kept on the shared shelf. The topic was deceptively narrow: how speakers **communicate** not just meaning but mood — how the same sentence, read **figuratively**, carries connotations no **sentential** analysis alone can capture.

Her argument was **persuasive** on the surface, but her committee had flagged a problem. One paragraph leaned so heavily on a famous theorist's phrasing that it edged toward **plagiarism**; she had, in effect, begun to **plagiarize** without realizing it, lifting the structure while swapping synonyms. She rewrote the section, this time letting the **vernacular** of her own field carry the weight — the informal, living **descriptive** language that practitioners actually use, not the polished register of translated theory. She worked to make every claim **unequivocal**, stripping out the **exaggerated** hedges that had crept in during tired late-night drafts. Where she had inserted a long **parenthesis** about historical context, she cut it to a single clause so the logic stayed tight and the **conjunction** between evidence and conclusion was clear.

The real trouble came during the defense. The **prolocutor** — a senior professor who chaired proceedings — pressed her on a slide. Had she used a **red herring** to sidestep a methodological flaw? She paused. The question carried **rhetorical** force designed to unsettle her. She recognized the **propaganda** move: frame the weakness as disqualifying before she could explain it. She refused to be distracted. Instead, she chose to **underscore** the one finding that mattered, **disseminate** its implications clearly across three fields, and **promulgate** a **proverbial** caution the committee itself had ignored: extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence. Her phrasing was careful — no **misstatement**, no **misinterpret**-able slide, no **incoherence** between data and conclusion. The **connotation** of every term had been weighed. When one examiner muttered that a rival paper was **full of crap**, the prolocutor said simply: **knock it off**. The room settled. She passed.

Later, reading the **transcript** of the session, she noticed how much of academic discourse depended on knowing when precision served truth and when it merely performed it.
:::

### When the Microphone Is Hot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The **valedictorian** stepped up to the podium, her notes loaded into the **teleprompter**, and cleared her throat. She had spent weeks polishing every line, swapping out **polysyllabic** tangents for plain, punchy sentences, because — as her coach liked to say — it goes **without further ado** that clarity beats cleverness in a packed auditorium. A foreign **correspondent** seated in the front row scribbled away, already framing her **complimentary** lead paragraph.

Backstage, the student emcee was practicing a **tongue twister** to warm up, pausing every few lines to let his **witty wordplay** land before moving on. The event program itself had required careful **disambiguation** — "address" meaning speech, not location — because the original draft had been nearly **unintelligible** to the volunteer translators working in three languages. English served as the de-facto **lingua franca** of the conference, bridging delegates who, **metaphorically** speaking, were sailing in very different waters. The simultaneous **interpretation** booth hummed quietly above them all.

When the ceremony finally began, the emcee warned the audience not to **blurt stuff out** during the citation readings. Applause, he reminded them, was the proper **acknowledgement** — a small but meaningful signal in a room where every word was being weighed. It goes **without further ado**, he added with a grin, and the crowd laughed, understanding him completely.
:::
